content: I'd like to help porting HeapLang, but I'm more comfortable with writing proofs rather than making design decisions. Are there some easy parts that need porting and are relevant for porting HeapLang?

suhr said:

I'd like to help porting HeapLang, but I'm more comfortable with writing proofs rather than making design decisions. Are there some easy parts that need porting and are relevant for porting HeapLang?

Thanks!
I will write a few things, and probably someone else can add more ideas.
I think until we have the weakest precondition, there might be only a few things to port wrt HeapLang:

  1. There's metatheory.v file that should not be blocked by anything.
  2. There's semantics of HeapLang. A few days ago I tried to provide an instance for the language interface here, but since there're no bit operations for integers in Lean standard library, I simply copied some definitions from Mathlib starting from here. However, I copied only the parts that were just enough to define evaluation. It would be nice to have a more systematic approach with lemmas about bit operations on integers, so that in future we could prove something about programs using them. If you are interested in it, it would be nice to have some integer bit operations as part of Iris Std.
What do you mean by bit operations for integers exactly? Does BitVec fit the bill? That is part of the standard library
I think what is missing is Nat.land, Nat.lor, Nat.xor and shifting for Int instead of Nat. I don't think that BitVec helps here.

Nat.land, Nat.lor and Nat.xor are defined in the standard library, and are what BitVec.and/or/xor are defined as! When you say, shifting for Int instead of Nat, do you mean the value being shifted, or the amount being shifted as the Int? Int.shiftRight, for example, exists as part of the standard library, but again, for BitVec we have sshiftRight, which performs an arithmetic right shift, hence treating the bitvector as a signed integer

I think we miss Int.land, Int.lor, Int.xor and shifts (left and right) for Int (both being shifted and the amount being shifted). I guess, one can implement them using BitVec (or as in Mathlib), but the important part is to have a self-contained module with relevant definitions/theorems, so that users of HeapLang are not exposed to implementation details of these operations, and can reason about them without unfolding.
I think the point Alex is trying to make is that instead of using Int, HeapLang could just use BitVec as its numeric data type. I've previously suggested this as well.

Something we need to figure out: is the point of HeapLang to have a 1-1 port of the Rocq version? I can imagine an argument for yes, to allow us to fairly compare Rocq vs Lean and to port logics that have only been described for HeapLang. Though I can also see the argument for not.

Relatedly, I'm of the opinion that HeapLeang can live in the math folder and reuse mathlib constructions. While I think it's good for the core library to have more flexibility in terms of their math dependencies, I would guess that logics depending on HeapLang will be more "whole cloth" Rocq ports and so the mathlib dependency is not as relevant. Just my 2c though, happy to hear other thoughts.

Henrik Böving said:

I think the point Alex is trying to make is that instead of using Int, HeapLang could just use BitVec as its numeric data type. I've previously suggested this as well.

I don't think I understand the suggestion. HeapLang's integers are infinite, i.e. exactly correspond to Int, but BitVec is finite as I understand it. How would you use BitVec without changing the semantics of HeapLang? Also it seems super confusing when you have a type Int in the standard library that models exactly what you want, but then you don't use it but some other type?

Markus de Medeiros said:

Something we need to figure out: is the point of HeapLang to have a 1-1 port of the Rocq version? I can imagine an argument for yes, to allow us to fairly compare Rocq vs Lean and to port logics that have only been described for HeapLang. Though I can also see the argument for not.

I think the HeapLang of Iris Lean should be a 1-1 port of the Rocq version such that people coming from Rocq have exactly the HeapLang they like and are used to. If people want to make their own version of HeapLang (as people also do all the time), they can do that.
I agree with Michael. 1-1 port of the HeapLang also would help using existing tutorials/other learning material.
Good! FWIW this is my opinion too :)

iris_heap_lang/primitive_laws.v depends on gen_heap, proph_map and gen_inv_heap, which depend on own.v. https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/issues/265 says that some of own.v is ported, but I can't find inG in Iris-Lean.

What exactly is ported and what needs to be? gen_heap and related parts don't seem to be too hard to port...

Lean version has a slightly different way to specify available resources. Instead inG, the Lean version uses something similar to subG, called ElemG in the codebase. One place to look on how to use it is https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/blob/master/Iris/Iris/Instances/Lib/WSat.lean. Most probably, gen_heap, proph_map and gen_inv_heap can be implemented similar to InvMapF from this file.
See also https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/pull/371 where there was a small discussion about that.
Thanks! I'll take a look.

Started porting ghost_map in https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/pull/407.

It seems like I'm entering the type class hell, and I would appreciate a bit of help on making inference work. Like, for some reason instance inference does not work for GhostMapG in my code, and I have to pass the instance explicitly.

Also, the fact that elements of a discrete OFE are discrete probably has a name in Rocq Iris, but I can't find it.
Thanks for taking it! I can take a look tomorrow.
Passing the instance around in the iOwn predicate seems to be common for our definition of iOwn
At least for the top-level predicates like you've defined in your PR
The problem is, nice syntax like "γ ↪◯MAP[k]{dq} v" does not work anymore in this case.

Meanwhile I tried to port Fractional as well, and have got a very weird type error:

class AsFractional {PROP: Type u} [bi: BI PROP] [UFraction F] (P : PROP) (Φ : F → PROP) (q : F)
  -- Invalid resulting type: Expected a sort
  -- as_fractional : ?m.2
  as_fractional : @BiEntails PROP (bi.toBIBase) P (Φ q)

For some reason Lean forgot how to infer types in this case and leaves a metavariable instead.
